newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU urges greater ambition for Singapore WTO.
newsitem.headline: EU urges greater ambition for Singapore WTO.

text.p: European Union foreign affairs ministers on Monday urged next month's Singapore meeting of World Trade Organisation leaders to push for more ambitious targets.
"They have agreed their draft conclusions which seek a more ambitious outcome than is currently in the Singapore draft declaration," a European Commission spokesman told reporters.
Ministers called for "strenuous efforts" from all WTO parties to tackle the EU's major topics of interest.

"(The EU) is of the opinion that more ambitious results in Singapore, in accordance with the priorities already established...would be in the interest of all participants," they said in their statement.

Ministers agreed last month to use Singapore to try to finalise agreements on trade and the environment, to push for international product standards, to protect intellectual property rights and to define globally accepted public procurement practices.
The bloc is also due to reaffirm its commitment to market liberalisation measures already agreed under the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) regime.
European Union ministers and officials are slated to meet on the spot at the Singapore ministerial to coordinate positions among members of the 15-country bloc.

While ministers on Monday appeared broadly united on tactics, Greece and Portugal sought "clearer language" on textiles trade issues while Sweden sought tougher provisions for world trade rules on investment and the environment.

France and Portugal pressed the Commission for its study on the legal conformity of the EU's growing number of bilateral trade agreements with WTO rules, which had been due for delivery to EU leaders at their Dublin summit next month.
"The Commission is making fun of us," a French diplomat told reporters in reference to the lack of progress with the report.
Asked whether the delay was deliberate, the diplomat said: "Yes, of course".

France, with an eye on its own farm sector, is concerned that EU bilateral trade deals, such as the one it is currently discussing with South Africa, may expose the bloc to legal challenges at the WTO.
